summary: This wiki note surveys institutes of technology and polytechnic-style institutions across several countries, contrasting them with academic universities. It covers Finland's ammattikorkeakoulu system, polytechnic education in Croatia, Pakistan, India, Venezuela, Thailand, Mauritius and Australia, including how their names, degree levels and admission routes differ. It also notes that several institutions renamed themselves 'University of Technology'.
one_line: Overview of institutes of technology and polytechnics worldwide, their degree structures, and how they differ from universities.
key_facts: Finland's polytechnics (ammattikorkeakoulu, Swedish yrkeshögskola) focus on degrees comparable in level to an academic bachelor's degree.
Finnish polytechnics have offered master's degrees (Master of Engineering) since 2006.
After January 1, 2006, some Finnish ammattikorkeakoulus translated their legal names as 'university of applied sciences' instead of 'polytechnic'.
The law about polytechnic education in Croatia was passed in 1997.
Polytechnic institutes in Pakistan offer a three-year diploma, with admission based on results in the 10th grade standardized exams.
Institutes of technology in Venezuela were developed in the 1950s as a post-secondary option in technical and scientific courses, modelled on French polytechnic concepts.
In India, a Diploma in Engineering is typically a three-year program offered after the tenth class by institutes affiliated with state boards of technical education.

Universities of Engineering & Technology in Pakistan grant Bachelor's degrees as 4-year full-time programs after 13 years of education, including the F.Sc, described as equivalent to the British A-Level.
Rajamangala University of Technology was formerly the Institute of Technology and Vocational Education in Thailand.
King Mongkut's University of Technology Thonburi was formerly the Thonburi Technology Institute.
The University of Technology, Mauritius is the only technical university in Mauritius, with its main campus at La Tour Koenig, Pointe aux Sables.

In Australia during the 1970s to early 1990s, 'institute of technology' described state-owned technical schools offering vocational and higher education within the College of Advanced Education system.
In the 1990s most Australian institutes of technology merged with existing universities or formed new ones, often taking the title 'University of Technology' for marketing rather than legal purposes.
The most prominent Australian technology university in each state founded the Australian Technology Network a few years later.
